title: Pathologist Salary Australia: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to calculate a pathologist salary Australia using hourly rates, award classifications, and the 38-hour week. Includes tax, super, and casual loading guidance.
salarySummary: A pathologist's minimum hourly rate in Australia depends on their award classification, with full-time ordinary earnings typically calculated at 38 hours per week for 52 weeks.

faqs.q: What is the minimum hourly rate for a pathologist in Australia?
faqs.a: Pathologists are covered by either the Health Professionals and Support Services Award or the Medical Practitioners Award, depending on their role. Minimum rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and published in the Modern Awards Pay Database. For the most accurate rate, check the relevant pay guide on the Fair Work Ombudsman website. As a general benchmark, the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, but award rates for health professionals are typically higher.

faqs.q: How do I convert a pathologist's hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time pathologist working 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. For example, at $50 per hour, annual gross pay would be $50 × 38 × 52 = $98,800. This assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. Superannuation is paid on top at 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base.

faqs.q: Does casual loading apply to pathologist salaries?
faqs.a: Yes, if a pathologist is employed as a casual, they are entitled to a casual loading of 25% on top of the minimum hourly rate. This is intended to compensate for not receiving paid leave. When using the [timesheet](/), you can check the 'casual loading' box to automatically add 25% to the base rate. The Fair Work Ombudsman states that casual employees must be paid at least the casual rate, which for the National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour from 1 July 2026.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Pathologist Salary Australia

When researching **pathologist salary Australia**, it's important to start with the correct minimum pay rates set by the Fair Work Commission and enforced by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Pathologists may be classified under the *Health Professionals and Support Services Award* or the *Medical Practitioners Award*, depending on their qualifications and duties. These awards specify minimum hourly rates, allowances, and penalty rates.

### The 38-Hour Week and Annual Conversion

Most full-time employees in Australia work a 38-hour week, as defined by the Fair Work Act. To convert an hourly rate to annual gross pay, use the formula:

**Annual gross = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time pathologist, this means:

- Hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual salary before tax and super.

For example, if a pathologist earns $60 per hour under their award, the annual gross pay is $60 × 38 × 52 = $118,560.

If you are paid fortnightly, your gross fortnight pay is simply the weekly amount multiplied by 2. For the above example, weekly pay is $2,280, so fortnightly is $4,560.

### Award Rates vs National Minimum Wage

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour for full-time and part-time employees, and $33.05 per hour for casuals (including 25% loading). However, most pathologists are covered by awards that set higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Commission's Modern Awards Pay Database provides the official minimum rates for each classification. Always check the relevant award before relying on general figures.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

If a pathologist works as a casual, they receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. This loading is meant to compensate for not receiving paid sick leave or annual leave. When using our [timesheet](/), you can select the 'casual loading' checkbox to automatically add 25% to the base rate you enter. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading—the tool adds it for you.

Superannuation is paid on top of ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026) up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For a pathologist earning $118,560 per year, the employer would contribute an additional $14,227.20 in super. This is not deducted from the employee's pay.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

For the 2026–27 financial year, resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners).

Using the example of $118,560 annual gross, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be approximately $27,000–$28,000, leaving a take-home pay of around $90,000–$91,000. For a more detailed breakdown, see our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide.

### Using Pay Guides and Reference Tables

The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes [pay guides](/blog) for each award, including the *Health Professionals and Support Services Award* and the *Medical Practitioners Award*. These guides list minimum hourly rates, allowances, and penalty rates. You can also use our [reference tables](/data) to compare award rates against the National Minimum Wage and ABS Average Weekly Earnings.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, full-time adult ordinary time earnings (May 2026) were $2,083.70 per week. This is a useful benchmark for comparing pathologist salaries to the broader workforce.

### Key Considerations

- The calculation above assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice.
- Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base.
- Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here.
- HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted.

This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax. For personalised advice, consult a qualified accountant or use the ATO's tax calculator.
